newsitem.title: USA: Tyson Foods head appears before grand jury.
newsitem.headline: Tyson Foods head appears before grand jury.

text.p: Don Tyson, the retired chairman of Tyson Foods Inc., testified on Thursday before a federal grand jury investigating allegations that a former Clinton administration agriculture secretary accepted gifts from companies he regulated.

Tyson's appearance came as the independent counsel tries to wrap up the grand jury's 30-month investigation into whether Mike Espy accepted free travel, football tickets and other favours from the giant food company. Some legal experts have suggested that Tyson or his company might also face indictments in the investigation.
Espy, who resigned in 1994, has repeatedly said he is innocent of any wrongdoing.
Tyson, 67, was expected to testify again on Friday, a spokesman said.

"It's our understanding that Don Tyson's testimony will continue tomorrow, and we won't have a statement until after then," said Archie Schaeffer, a spokesman for Tyson Foods, based in Fayetteville, Ark.

Tyson lives in semi-retirement in Arkansas. His poultry company has had close ties to Bill Clinton since the 1980s when Clinton was governor of the state. Tyson was a regular contributor to Clinton's political campaigns.
A spokesman for independent counsel Donald Schmaltz declined comment on the grand jury probe.
"We don't comment at all on things that happen with the grand jury," spokesman Charles Blakley said. "We've said before that we're trying to conclude the investigative phase of our work."

In March, a federal jury convicted Jack Williams, a former lobbyist for Tyson Foods, for lying during the investigation of Espy. Williams is scheduled to be sentenced on June 5, and faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Investigators said Williams tried to mislead them about his role in Espy's invitation to a Dallas Cowboys play-off game in January 1994 as a guest of Tyson Foods.
Espy later repaid the cost of the football ticket to avoid any appearance of impropriety, the Tyson Foods spokesman said.

The investigation began after questions were raised about Espy's acceptance of gifts from Tyson Foods at the same time the U.S. Agriculture Department was preparing tighter meat and poultry inspection rules.
More than a dozen individuals and companies, including Espy's former chief of staff, have been indicted in the probe.

The White House has refused to turn over documents sought by the grand jury, claiming executive privilege. A federal appeals court in Washington is expected to rule soon on the subpoenas, but the court's decision will be sealed because of the secret nature of grand jury investigations.

The Espy probe has unfolded quietly compared to a separate investigation led by independent counsel Kenneth Starr into the Clintons' links to a failed Arkansas savings and loan and the Whitewater real estate venture.
